claims.text: Initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are homogeneously mixed when prepared under standard synthesis conditions.
Preferential Cu surface segregation governs the onset and progression of melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Cu segregation occurs at temperatures below the nominal bulk melting point.
Surface-segregated Cu forms a Cu-rich, liquid-like layer before bulk melting.
The Cu-rich liquid-like surface layer nucleates and accelerates melting of the underlying alloy.
The constituent metals have disparate melting temperatures.
Cu has the lowest melting point among Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, and Cu.
Cu's lower melting point causes it to segregate to the nanoparticle surface as temperature increases.
A Cu-rich surface region has a lower melting barrier than the underlying alloy.
Minimal passivation can suppress Cu surface segregation without significantly changing thermal conductivity.
Suppressing Cu segregation will delay melting or make melting more spatially uniform.
Unshelled particles will develop a distinct Cu-rich liquid surface layer before nominal bulk melting.
Minimally passivated particles will lack localized premelting or show significantly delayed and more uniform melting relative to unshelled particles.
Unshelled, as-synthesized FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles naturally exhibit Cu surface-segregation dynamics during heating.
Above their melting temperature, metallic components can enter a liquid phase and form molten beads whose behavior is influenced by surface-energy minimization.
